text: If you don't turn a person lying still to the right and to the left, their body starts to break down under its own weight.
This vital rule, used in intensive care today, was written word for word in Surah Al-Kahf, fourteen hundred years ago.
In verse eighteen of Surah Al-Kahf, describing the young men asleep in the cave, Allah says:
You would have thought they were awake, although they were asleep. We turned them over on their right and left sides, while their dog stretching its forelegs at the entrance.
Surah Al-Kahf, verse eighteen.
Notice the detail in this verse.
We turned them over on their right and left sides.
In a story about people asleep, why does it stress that they were turned to the right and to the left?
Modern medicine and intensive care know very well how vital this sentence is.
When a person lies still in the same position for a long time, the blood vessels caught between the weight of the bones and the surface beneath get blocked.
Oxygen no longer reaches the tissue.
Soon, tissue death and clotting begin. Medicine calls it a decubitus ulcer, or a bedsore.
In intensive care, the most basic rule for keeping an unconscious patient alive is to turn them to the right and to the left at regular intervals.
There is one more detail.
While the verse says the young men were turned to the right and to the left, of their dog it says: stretching its forelegs.
So the dog is not turned.
Then why are the people turned, but not the dog?

Because, as veterinary anatomy shows, when a dog lies down on its chest with its forelegs stretched out in front, in the sphinx position, its weight spreads evenly across its broad chest, and its blood vessels are not squeezed.
In this special position, no bedsores form on the dog's body.
The turning that protects people from tissue death, and the special posture that protects the dog's vessels.
Follow for more of the Quran's fine details like this.
